The Record of the Deeds of Dharma Master Lianfa After His Passing (Minggao) Yu Zhi praises the virtues of the Elder Master Ci; (Yizheng) Chen Zejing transmits [this account]. **The Record of the Deeds of Dharma Master Lianfa After His Passing** [The following is the translated text: The Master’s name was Lianfa, his secular surname being Wang. He was a native of Wuxi. From his youth, he possessed a profound disposition for the Way and a sincere mind for the Dharma. At the age of twenty-one, he left home to become a monk under the guidance of the Venerable Master Xuanzong of the Huayan Monastery on Mount Jiuhua. He diligently applied himself to the study of the Vinaya and the Mahāyāna sutras. Later, he traveled to various regions to seek out the teachings, eventually arriving at the Lingyan Monastery in Yizheng, where he took up residence. Master Lianfa was renowned for his compassionate nature and his dedication to the salvation of sentient beings. He constantly exhorted others to cultivate merit and virtue, never tiring of his efforts. During the years of the Republic, as the world was in turmoil, he remained steadfast in his practice, never wavering from his vows. He maintained a simple and austere lifestyle, relying solely on alms to sustain himself. In the spring of the year 1948, the Master fell ill. Despite his ailment, he continued to preach the Dharma and encourage his disciples with great vigor. On the night of the eighth day of the fourth lunar month, he passed away peacefully while seated in meditation. He was seventy-three years of age. His passing was met with deep sorrow by those who had known him. Subsequently, his remains were enshrined in a stupa at the Lingyan Monastery. His disciples compiled this record to commemorate his life and to ensure that his legacy would endure for generations. May his merits be vast and his compassion eternal, benefiting all beings throughout the ten directions. *Recorded by Yu Zhi of Wuxi, praising the virtues of the Elder Master Ci; and Chen Zejing of Yizheng.*

The Separate Biography of Seng Xinjing (Yizheng): Yu Yanghao. Xinjing’s courtesy name was Ruheng;

He once made a vow for the Pure Land together with Yōkō and Gyokushaku; furthermore, while at Shukendō Cave with Gyokushaku, he made a vow to deliver sentient beings. His resolve was most magnificent.

He delighted in performing meritorious deeds for the benefit of others. When practicing the Yoga *Vaśitā* (Feeding the Hungry Ghosts) ritual, he often remarked with wonder: "The Pure Land is entered through sound;

this is the most wondrous expedient. Whenever his heart was stirred, he would lead the chanting of praises and prostrations, or kneel to recite the accounts of the twenty-five sages of the Universal Gate who described their own lives.

Biography of Dafugenfu (Dafu Kuai).
Dafu Kuai was a bhikṣu of Tianzhang Dajue Temple. He received full ordination at Chengtian Temple in Gaoyou and passed away at Fangsheng Temple.
When he was ill and medical treatments were ineffective, he single-mindedly turned his heart toward the Western Flower Pond and let go of his life.

Songyuan Chuan Da-gen:
Songyuan was the son of the Zhu family of Gaoyou. From childhood, he suffered from an illness for which medical treatment proved ineffective. One night, he dreamed of a divine being who said to him:
He said, "You must leave the secular world; only then can your illness be cured. Upon waking, he immediately made a vow, and his disease was indeed healed.

Following Master Pūrṇa, he left the household life and received full ordination at the Eight-Treasure Avalokiteśvara Temple. He took up residence at the Locust King Temple east of the city and practiced asceticism.
He diligently cultivated the Pure Land and led the assembly in the recitation of the Buddha’s name to such an extent that he forgot both sleep and food.

One night, a petty thief scaled the wall and approached his bedside, searching through everything; yet as Songyuan was focused on visualizing the Lotus Pond, he remained indifferent and did not inquire about him.

To all people he spoke no other words, but only exhorted them to recite the Buddha’s name with a single-minded resolve. Both children and the elderly were all transformed by his guidance. (Tongzhi Wuchen)
In the middle of winter, he fell ill. Several days prior, he addressed the fourfold assembly, saying: "I am about to depart. Do not grieve or feel attachment;

An Anonymous Account of a Practicing Monk:

A certain monk resided in the capital, his stature as lofty and white as a mountain peak. Those who encountered him often observed that he was simple and rustic in manner, devoted to ascetic practice, and his aspirations were fixed upon the Western Land.
At the time of his death, he departed with serene composure; throughout his life, he harbored neither affliction nor resentment, and thus attained such a fruit.

His temperament was broad and magnanimous. He presided over Zifu Monastery for over twenty years, serving the Dharma and sentient beings with tireless diligence and earnest devotion.

He retired from his seat to travel abroad, where he brought about immense spiritual transformation. He resided in a single room within the temple, severing all worldly ties to cultivate purity; he remained unchanged through both cold and heat.

In the second year of the Xianfeng era, he returned to the temple to escape the Red Turbans. Foreknowing that his time had come, he passed away while sitting cross-legged without illness at the age of sixty-eight.
Fuyuan Chuan-da Genfuyuan resided at Shagou in Yancheng.
While chanting sutras for the sake of fellow monks, there were sometimes instances of negligence or omission.
Whenever this occurred, Fuyuan would return to the temple and invariably chant the entire text once more to compensate for the deficiency. He did so even during the dead of night or in bitter cold.

Thus it was. As he approached old age, he focused his mind single-mindedly on the Pure Land, reciting the Buddha’s name with a fixed number of repetitions. He practiced with such diligence for eight years that, at the time of his death, while holding his prayer beads and chanting the Buddha’s name, he cast the beads aside and passed away.
*An Account of a Certain Monk* (Wulin), by Gao Yuan.

As he wandered through the temple grounds, his condition improved. His family then provided him with the means to leave the household life; he took Fayuan as his master and received full ordination on Mount Hua.

He maintained his vows and practices with diligence and traveled extensively to visit famous mountains. After forty days, he presided over Fengyang Temple and conferred the precepts for thirteen sessions, causing those who were transformed by his teachings to increase in number.
Over time, he became thoroughly proficient in both Buddhist and secular classics; whenever he had a moment’s leisure from reading, he would immediately engage in the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
His followers constantly numbered in the tens of thousands. When the Red Turbans rose in rebellion, he took refuge at Putuo Rock for eight years before returning.
On the eighth day of the first month of the Jisi year of the Tongzhi era, he said to his disciples, "I shall depart forty days from now.
Immediately, a craftsman came to construct a coffin. When the assembly asked why he had suddenly appeared, the craftsman replied, "A junior disciple called for me," though in truth this was not so.
He was a junior disciple. When the appointed time arrived, he bathed, changed his robes, and moved his seat to the side of the hall.
He lit incense in the burner and said, "When this incense smoke is exhausted, I shall depart from this Sahā world. Shortly thereafter, it was exactly as he had said.
Biographical Draft of Songdo (宗道): Great Root Songdo.

A native of Hae-ryeong, he entered the monastic life at Pobo Hermitage. He was renowned for his ascetic practices and steadfast integrity. Constantly mindful of the gravity of the Buddha’s grace, he vowed to offer his own body as a repayment.

He rescued the ignorant and deluded, leading them from heterodoxy to the correct path. Moved by his transformative influence, even butchers were converted.

Together with several like-minded companions, he established a Buddha-recitation hall and diligently cultivated the practices of the Pure Land for four years. Whenever others lacked necessities, he extended his own resources to them; thus, through toil and hardship, he persevered.

He passed away from a slight illness in the first year of the Guangxu era at the age of sixty-six.
Biographical Draft of Xi’an:

Baoqian devoted himself deeply to the principles of the Buddha, vowing to dedicate his entire life to this pursuit.

Among the gentry and commoners, there were many who turned their hearts toward him in reverence and admiration. In receiving junior disciples, his kindness and compassion surpassed those of others. Later, he retired from his seat to travel to various regions to study under other masters.
He finally passed away at Qianhua from a slight illness. His remains were cremated, and several grains of śarīra were obtained.
These events took place in the first year of the Xianfeng era; he was fifty-six years of age.

He was able to provide offerings for the pure monk Qingche while the latter remained in retreat for three years; this is especially difficult for human nature to endure.

He delighted in performing the *yoga* *yankou* (fire-mouth) food-offering ritual alone and maintained the *Dabei zhou* (Great Compassion Mantra). He was swift and incisive in his practice, and his friendship with Nianzang was exceptionally deep.
It is said that because Nianzang’s mind was pure and lucid, he also frequently associated with the monks carving the scriptures.
These monks often wished to offer him a dose of "cooling medicine" to quench the thirst of his parched belly, yet they had not yet succeeded. His verse says:

"Wandering through every land within the body, Years pass by, whether long or short. The Avataṃsaka is not something newly fashioned; The Ocean-Seal manifests as perfect bubbles. Loyalty, filial piety, and the immortal."
A dream: the conditions for wisdom, brilliance, wealth, and nobility. In the upright realm of Dīpaṃkara, the bright mirror reflects the mists of the nine provinces.

Body and body dwell in mutual interplay; the spirit of the body makes the activities of the body spiritual. Within a single hair, the earth-vessels revolve; within a speck of dust, the sutras of emptiness turn.

With movement and stillness, one transcends the three realms; its radiant glory reveals but a single star. Such supernormal powers are not something small; they flow with all things in cool, refreshing clarity. Do not treat this as mere "suchness."

Unraveling the silken threads, it draws forth wondrous light; within a single hair-pore, a great world-system is contained. Abiding in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one dwells as the Sovereign of Space.

I roam within this realm with you—what person is not by your side? Those who are noisy and base merely exhaust themselves in vain. Beyond the heavens, there is originally fragrance; how could there be a Buddha attained through cultivation?
Toiling in vain with anxieties in dreams, why do devas and humans remain so distressed? The waters of the sea flow on of their own accord. Do not study like an Arhat...

Han: Who is the prisoner of the state of Chu? Radiance is ever liberated. Desiring to seize it, one startles the gulls; The Dharma-realm is vast, yet time is tight. Not even a hair’s breadth can be deceived.
Coming from within illusion to drink wine, Beyond emptiness, one observes the game of chess by oneself. Who determines the weight of brush and ink? How could the passage of time be fast or slow?
Possessing alone the nature of equality, I send this up upon a branch of green willow. Contemplating phenomena, they truly come to fruition.
A set of robes; Zen meditation has ultimately proven ineffectual. Amidst my daily activities, I sit alone; in the midst of clamor, I constantly listen to the sutras.
Pale colors hold within them deep hues; the star of gold transforms into the star of jade. Infinite matters of dreams and spirits—few are those who would listen as I speak of them.

With a singular, vast and profound intent, my mind is already weary with care. Who can discourse upon the six marks? Having no concerns, I simply take my three meals. A flowering branch emerges from the Buddha.
Manifestation: the empty mirror of the mind contains reflected images; even a young child finds this most delightful, as the ball and the dance intersect spontaneously.

When self and other employ one another, how wondrous! All is the Buddha. Those with false penetration shrink back in hesitation; deluded by suffering, they wish to rush about. Today there is originally nothing to do;
let us simply sing a song in leisure. A bright mirror hangs across the sky; each and every part has been freshly polished. Even one or two remain complete.

Delusion! Why labor to calculate existence and non-existence? The discriminations made within a dream bring weariness; once awakened, one’s nature and character remain as they were. Who created the snow and rain, and over what years and months?

Who caused the errors of "lu" and "yu" in the texts? All is clearly present before the eyes; ten thousand times drawing gourds [from memory] turns this entire *Śrī-vyūha-sūtra* into a landscape of broken traces.
Since even the mark of a true self does not exist, who is there to receive the grace of the Dharma King? The scripture scrolls are but empty dust.
Miscellaneous. The radiance of dreams and awakening remains; why cling to it with such bitterness? Let the body fly and dance through the universe.

A Brief Account of the Awakening by Dong Jingkong (Changzhou).
Wukai resided at Tiantong Temple in Changzhou. Throughout his life, he devoted himself solely to practical cultivation. He did not eat after noon and never lay down on his back at night.
He constantly sat in a single room, diligently reciting the Buddha’s name. Whenever any of his disciples sent him offerings, he would invariably refuse them.
A few days before his death, he took leave of all his friends. When the appointed time arrived, his countenance was bright and clear, and he was free from any suffering.
In an instant, he passed away. Shortly thereafter, he opened his eyes again and said, "I have just gone out of the temple gate, reached the wooden bridge, and returned.

Now I am going straight to the Western Land. Having finished speaking, he became silent. Previously, there had been a vow to build a stupa that remained unfulfilled; after his passing, [the matter was settled] in Shanghai.

I, disciple [Name], witnessed my Master entrust me with the affairs of the stupa and monastery. More than a month later, when I took my funds and traveled to Taining, I learned that my Master had already passed away.
Among the assembly, there was none who did not sigh in wonder at this event, which occurred during the Tongzhi era.

Delighted, I offer this eulogy. The annotation to the *Changzhou Fu* states: "Guangji, surnamed Feng, originally named Shixi, later changed his name to Dingzhong. He was selected in the provincial examination of the Wuli year (1605).

He donated Xiyuan Garden to organize the release of living beings (*fangsheng*) for the public and established the Shifang An (Ten Directions Hermitage) to welcome travelers from afar. He devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land Buddhism and exhorted others [to do the same]."

He abstained from slaughtering animals; he would kneel and weep whenever he encountered them. During the summer months, he did not drive away mosquitoes, lying instead amidst reeds and rushes, allowing them to bite his skin at will. He built a stupa at Foshouwa on Mount Hua.
Observing the timing and discerning the momentum, I cast aside glory to seek the withered. The lotus flower is fragrant; Its blossoming is ever more lush.
Self and others are of one essence; Subject and object are entirely so. With resolute spirit, I unfold this discourse;
Benevolent words spread their benefit. Alas! This wondrous joy of the gourd is a true pearl.
The Chapter on Amitābha Buddha: The Moon.
Amitābha is that which is equally possessed by the hearts of every single person.

When one reaches the ultimate state of total forgetfulness, apart from these four characters "A-mi-t'o-fo," there is nothing further lacking and nothing further superfluous; yet people consequently [regard] Amitābha...

The Buddha’s naming of him was indeed extraordinary. At the North Gate of Taizhou, at the Monastery of the Gonghou Temple, there was a monk named Rui-tang. He lived in solitude yet possessed pure virtue;

he accepted food and clothing as they came, never seeking abundance, and would not step foot anywhere except in accordance with the precepts. Free from desire and worldly pursuit, none in the world could fathom him. Whenever he observed the phenomena of the world, he sighed deeply, saying:
"This body is like a drifting duckweed; its coming and going are exceedingly easy. He said to his fellow practitioners: [and so forth].

Those who admire the Way and cherish benevolence find it present in every category of things. The errors of worldly people arise from the ease with which their affections are stirred and their resolve is not firm.

(Whenever I have dealings with families who favor Buddhism, even if it be midday or I am weary of spirit, I would simply enter their rooms and lie down. Upon waking, I would depart with carefree ease, completely forgetting all regard for social prohibitions. The worldly people, in turn, never showed the slightest concern for such impropriety. How extraordinary!)
In the eighth month of the Ji-mao year, he suffered a slight illness. Sitting upright upon his straw mat, he recited the name of Amitābha;
his physical form and breath remained harmonious and tranquil as he passed away at the Tidyu Hermitage. He was seventy-eight years of age.

In the eastern land, the layman Chikyō Ō (偶) of Keijūkan Rōjin (慶咫觀老人),
who served as a senior official,
initially did not believe in the Buddha. For several years, however, he had been secretly praying to Amitābha for his compassionate protection.
He traveled to the Zhejiang provincial examination center. Accompanying the Elder to Upper Tianzhu, he was moved by the hidden power of Avalokiteśvara.
That evening, the Elder dreamed that a courtyard of flowers had blossomed; holding a half-tail of *shíyú* fish against a jade ruler, he was about to cook it.
Over the course of one hundred days, he resolved his mind to recite the Buddha’s name and gradually ceased using tobacco, alcohol, and meat. He then diligently studied the Mahāyāna scriptures.

Ji stayed at Ganma Village for nearly ten years. There was a rat in his host’s house that silently received his transformative influence; it passed away while sitting in meditation, remaining incorruptible.
The old man took it back home, adorned it with gold, and offered a single stick of incense daily, saying, "This, too, was a spiritual friend."
To this day, the image of the rat remains at Haitian Jingsha (also known as Fangsheng An). Those who cultivate pure karma frequently behold it;
many are moved to sigh with deep emotion and feel a sense of shame and gratitude.
The centipede said, "The living beings of the Jade Purity Realm derive benefit from humanity. Although their spirits and forms may differ for a time, the true light of successive kalpas is impartial.
To plant but a single seed and yet attain heights that touch the heavens—this is not at all strange. [This was spoken] within the Lotus Pond of the Pure Land.
He was a man. Once, as he went out his gate, he saw a child using a bamboo-slip bow to shoot centipedes. Moved by pity, he ransomed their lives.
Later, when he preached the Dharma to guests by a lotus pond, the centipedes would come to listen. This continued for many years, not as a mere coincidence;
it was clear that they had long since been transformed into the wondrous forms of devas and humans, hastening toward the Pure Land.
The transformed bird is a divine being capable of transcending both purity and defilement;
it speaks of Li Sheng, who possesses the prajñā-mind yet cannot achieve transcendence. His eloquence is sharp and his roots of goodness are manifest, yet he is bound by the illusion of evil karma.
Having lost the human body through error, he was reborn as a celestial bird that preached the Dharma.

Like the elephant of Śakra, his supernatural powers were entirely equal to those of the devas, surpassing the reach of other divine elephants. As a preeminent leader among the nāga kings, he had transcended to a superior stage and remained with further potential.
Devas and spirits intermingled, such that it was impossible to discern the true from the false. It was not only birds in the West who were transformations of Amitābha.
It is simply so. Furthermore, when Amitābha Buddha enters the thirty-seven sacred maṇḍalas, he changes his name to Avalokiteśvararāja;
he then rides upon a peacock to symbolize sovereignty and does not sit upon a lotus. This bird and this Buddha—
"Is it one, or is it two? O Mahāśrī-devī, all is pure; naturally there appears a six-tusked white elephant.
With its trunk, it grasps a *maṇi* jar and pours forth various precious jewels, which drench the crown of [the king's] head. Moreover, from where does this come?
It has been said that the Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) is sovereign among all ordinary beings, and his pure and spiritual retinue serves as the treasury of his army."
As for the various artisans, they are transformed into the likeness of elephants, horses, and so forth.

These five classes of sentient beings, although they shared the same vows as the Wheel-Turning Kings in the past, differ greatly from them in their conduct and practice. (Furthermore, as in the case of the One-Syllable Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin, who manifests the seven treasures at will, these male and female sentient beings are neither real nor unreal;
they consist purely of both the holy and the ordinary. Nevertheless, within these transformations, each one possesses its own cause.)
Those who ride the divine vehicle of the wheel of vows and transcend both purity and defilement do so by relying on the accomplishment of other-power (*tariki*);
perhaps they themselves do not realize it. In this world, there are those who love birds, cats, mice, and dogs;

yet they regret that they have been unable to transform this affectionate mind into the contemplation of their beloved sentient beings as syllable-seeds of red glass color, thereby leading them to become members of the Lotus family. Or...
If one enters among the categories of beings and becomes their leader, one will obtain a superior reward; truly, those who remain base and inferior are pitiable.
Read as *hṛīḥ* (a compound syllable). Contemplate that this is the seed-syllable of the Lotus Family of Amitābha Buddha; it is most great.
